utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I will be calling the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may do that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mr. Gasi. MR. ISAK GASI, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you take that oath, please, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In translation]: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Isak Gasi.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5th May 1957.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to offer the next in line Prosecution exhibit, I believe it would be Prosecution Exhibit 73.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I ask that the usher please take it from you and give it to the representative from the Registry who will mark it as 73.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could show that to the Defence as well, please? If that could be placed on the projector, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Prosecution Exhibit 73?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 73 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Gasi, could you please look at Prosecution Exhibit 73 and would you for the court please point to Brcko, the area from which you come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you indicate, please, and point on to the projector? Thank you. Mr. Gasi, what Opstina is Brcko in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before, it was the assembly of the municipality of Brcko before the war.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you from the town of Brcko or a village within the Opstina of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the town of Brcko, from the centre, from the centre itself.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Brcko borders on what former Republic and now a country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: North, there is the Sava River which separates us from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did you live in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the date of my birth until I left the city on 7th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you know, could you tell us the ethnic composition of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority population in the municipality and in the town were Bosnian Muslims, Croats came the next and the third group of population were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, what was your prior occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked for Elektrodistribucija Brcko for 15 years, that is, I was an electrician.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You worked there until what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Till 27th May when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: '92, May 1992, the 27th May.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked on the control and the maintenance of this equipment in the territory of the municipality of Brcko, I mean, electrical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did your duties carry you to areas of Opstina other than the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, throughout the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there any sports that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, rowing -- canoe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At what levels did you participate in this sport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a rather high level in the old Yugoslavia and outside Yugoslavia, somewhere in the middle, shall we say, I was in the middle in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you also participated at the international level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As a result of your sports activities would you say that you were well known or, at least, known throughout Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever engage in any military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, regularly I served in the regular Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October 1977 to December 1978.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you perform that service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, we had training in Kraljevo and then they were sent to Prokuplje, that is, traffic something, what was it called, in Serbia, in the central part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where is Kraljevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, it is the central part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Driver.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During your service in the military did you become familiar with JNA uniforms, weapons, equipment and markings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to your military service in Serbia, were you in Belgrade for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as an athlete and I also studied there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Over what period of time did you study in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 79 to '81, two years, three years and a half, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As a result of your military service and your study in Serbia, did you become familiar with Serb dialects and accents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the period 1990 through 1992 did you notice the establishment of political parties in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What political parties were established in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically in the town of Brcko I know the party for Democratic Action, Croatian Democratic Union, Serb Democratic Party, and Former Communists, the Social Democratic Party. These were the larger ones.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there any acronyms that were used for those parties such as SDA or HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I gave you their full names but, yes, these are their acronyms, SDA, HDZ, SDS, SDP.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you a member of any of those parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What party was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you hold any position in that party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A member of the town's Executive Committee of the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I attended meetings; I did not have any special duties.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the elections that were held in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to those elections did you attend any rallies or meetings at which Serb spokesmen made remarks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall one such meeting at which Mr. Karadzic was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he was there twice. He was there at the founding assembly of SDS and I think there was also an election rally of SDS.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any comments which Mr. Karadzic made pertaining to Serb unity or nationalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What comments do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one commentary which impressed me which I remembered about the red colour in the Serbian flag and he commented on that, as of that red colour representing the blood shed by the Serb people, by the Serb people during that joint Yugoslavia and before that. That is something that left an impression on me, that it should not happen again to the Serb people, and that that should never happen again. The Serbs should not allow it again. That is something that I think he commented or, rather, spoke.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At the elections that were held in Brcko in 1990, who won in the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Former Communists, SDP.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As a result of that victory by the Communist party, did the other parties form a coalition against the Communist party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The three national parties.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions concerning the leadership in Brcko after these elections. Who was the President of the Assembly there after the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A member of SDA, of the party of the Muslim people, Mustafa Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And a representative of what party became a President of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A representative of the SDS, Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The police organisation in Brcko, is it correct that it was organised into two departments or units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was the regular police and the State Security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it has always been like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After these elections, what party representative held the position of chief of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the State Security Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Always, I mean before the war, it was always a Serb, and when the war was beginning that Serb retired and the one who succeeded him was again a Serb. I do not know if he was a member of the SDS but he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At the time of the elections in Brcko, did the Territorial Defence exist there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was the head of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milutinovic Milisav.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you know, what was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of the positions that we have discussed, based on your understanding of the power structure in the Opstina, which positions held the most power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should say Bosnians and Muslims after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As to the positions themselves between, for example, the President of the Assembly and the President of the Executive Council, which was the most powerful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The office of the Mayor of the President of the Opstina ranks first, but the Executive power was in the hands of the representative of the SDS because he was the President of the Executive Council of the municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, these people we have spoken of, did they remain in these positions in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of the police officers on the police Force in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the composition of the police Force in Brcko, as far as the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were Serbs even before the war under the old regime and when the elections were over.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time period 1991 and 1992, did you become aware of the creation of any new Serbian autonomous region around the area of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you become aware of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went to work, when I went on my regular rounds, I moved around those areas but they were Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How do you know that there was this Serb autonomous region in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was written on some of the roadsigns in paint, and when I went towards Bijeljina there was SAO Semberija and Majevica on the road immediately after leaving the town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did Brcko itself become a part of this Serb autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I used to go out of the town there were no slogans or notices of that kind in that town. It was only on the outskirts of the town that one saw the roadsigns they had written that that was where that region was beginning, that that was the entrance into the region.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the time period 1991, do you recall the military mobilization of Serb men in the area of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was, there were summons by the municipality's Secretariat for national defence, they were sending summons to men who served on the reserve JNA units. It was sometime towards the late, towards the end of 1990 in my municipality is when it began.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that mobilization call, do you recall seeing many men in Serb villages wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reserve uniforms of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see the same thing in Muslim villages with many men wearing these JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not see them. There was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the time period February and March 1992, do you recall the referendum for independence being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the question that was posed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be 100 per cent sure and quote the questions, but roughly it said: "Are you for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina composed of Muslims, Serbs and Croats?", something to that effect. I think it was taken over from the old constitution which already was in existence, that is, one of 1991 and you could vote for or against.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to the referendum itself, did you attend any rallies or meetings at which Serb leaders spoke about this referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the Serb leaders who were present at any of these rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, yes, they were there, many of them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you remember being there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was Mr. Karadzic at the time, the representative of the Serb Democratic Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Nikola Koljevic, Mr. Aleksa Buha, Maksimovic. I think the entire leadership of that main board of SDS attended one of those rallies.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any occasion when a minister from Belgrade also attended one of these rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall his position, how it was described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called him, those who announced the speakers, they announced him, they called him Minister for Trans Drinaic Serbs or the Serbs across the Drina. His name was Mr. Cvetic or Cvetinovic. I cannot remember exactly but that was roughly what it was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you understand what they meant by Minister for Serbs across the Drina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To whom was he referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were those -- our Bosnian Serbs and, I guess, Krajina Serbs, that is, those who were not in the Republic of Serbia but outside the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the Drina is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the border between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia in the old Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the comments that were made at any of these rallies by these Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, among other things as I listed them, Mr. Karadzic said that nobody had the right to separate the Serb people from their mother country, he meant Serbia, I presume; that no referendum or, I do not know what his words were, but no referendum, no force. They did not recognise, or something to that effect. Many of them spoke roughly about that at that rally, at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to this referendum itself, did you make any public pronouncements on the topic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, twice, I think.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less, I advocated, I spoke for common life because Yugoslavia as it existed before was no more, so that we should try to live together in Bosnia again, irrespective of the ethnic origin or religion. That was the gist of my interview on Sarajevo television and at the local television station in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After this referendum, what was the reaction of the Serb leaders in the Brcko area to the results of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were no any outbursts in the town, as far as I know. I attended a couple of local rallies of the Serb Democratic Party, and those of local Brcko leaders of the Serb people; repeated what I had already mentioned, what Mr. Karadzic and that Minister for the Serbs across the Drina used to say.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that nobody could separate the Serb people from their mother country Serbia, that nobody had the right to do it, and that Serb people had said what they wanted and that the Serb people wanted to live in peace with their neighbours, but if that failed that there would be another way. These would be roughly the quotations that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what military installations were there in the town of Brcko itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a garrison of the Yugoslav People's Army in the town, and then nearby, that is, close to the company where I worked, there were the training grounds and warehouses and hangars, depots, for heavy artillery and vehicles, and there was another warehouse in a village some 10 kilometres out of town on the other side of the town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was your home in connection to this garrison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, next to the garrison itself. My house was next to the garrison. My back garden overlooked the garrison, for some 50 to 100 metres from the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was your work in relation to this other training area and equipment storage area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The training area was across the road. There was only the road between my company and them, and the garages for heavy vehicles were on the same road, perhaps up to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time period 1990 through 1992, did you notice any increase in weapons, equipment or military convoys moving into the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were passing through the town. As of the end of 1990, I do not know, I presume as they were withdrawing from Croatia and they were moving towards Bijeljina, and some stayed in the town in those garages and some went on passing my company and towards Bijeljina. There were many convoys.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In those convoys what did you notice as far as troops, equipment or weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, tanks were loaded on those big transporters and then guns and some radio communications, components, elements were drawn by JNA vehicles, and there were also rockets but we could see them in part. I presume they are anti-aircraft. There were very many convoys which passed through the town, and there was army also. Every second day there would be one or two convoys passing through the town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise the equipment, weapons and the vehicles in these convoys as JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that some of this equipment moving through the town remained in the town. What types of equipment or weapons remained in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I saw were the garage facilities that were full overnight, became full overnight, with some very large guns. They were visible. They were not hidden and there at the training areas there were guns, quite a number of them. I do not know. The armoured vehicles, all this was the JNA weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992 do you recall seeing weapons or equipment in Serb villages surrounding Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you happen to be able to see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, because of the nature of the work I did, I had to go in those Serb villages, and I had to take care of the electrical appliances in some important facilities.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What types of weapons and equipment did you see in these villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All kinds of weaponry that the JNA used to have, tanks, the guns of all calibre, then armoured vehicles, motor vehicles for special purposes, like, for example, some communications vehicles, then first aid vehicles. All of them wore the marks, the insignia of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this same time period did you see any similar weapons or equipment in any of the Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I had not seen them. They were not there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again in the spring of 1992, did you notice the establishment of any checkpoints around the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did you first see these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it must have been mid 1991, yes, somewhere mid 1991, it started.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: They continued to exist there through the spring of '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you see these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the town, but outside of the town at the access, road access towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military policemen of the JNA and also the civilian policemen from the municipality of Brcko, that is, the Secretariat for the Interior of the municipality of Brcko which was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to these checkpoints at the access to the town of Brcko, did you see any other checkpoints in the Opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were those located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The access leading to Serb villages in the area of the Brcko municipality, there were checkpoints of the military police of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the spring of 1992, did you see any Serbs in the Brcko area being given weapons and fuel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of them had already the weapons and the JNA uniforms, and especially I was there when they were distributing weapons to the civilians in the villages like Srpska Gredica or a suburban part of town where 100 per cent of the Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were there and saw this, tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that part called Srpska Gredica, there was a JNA truck, TAM 5005D -- that was the make -- was parked there in front of this local office, and the local civilians from that village were there in a row and the weapons were distributed from the boxes that were taken out of the truck. There were three or four officers; one of them was a lieutenant from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the other area, you said one of these Serb areas of the town, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Potocari, yes, that is a suburban commune there; they were distributing the weapons to the civilians, to my neighbours. I lived very near that particular commune.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again who were the people who were distributing the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army. There was always an officer there and two soldiers, one driver and maybe several other soldiers. They were always present there. I even saw what they call the armour registry books. For every rifle that had to be distributed, those people had to acknowledge with a receipt. That was the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see a similar distribution of weapons in any of the Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again during the spring of 1992, did you ever see any military helicopters land near your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They landed in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was this that you saw this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it must have started somewhere towards the end of 1991, and then it started to be more frequent at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall one occasion when a helicopter landed at the barracks and individuals wearing red berets got out of the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, of course I remember. I know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about a month before the conflict started in my town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise the helicopter to be a JNA helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was marked that it was JNA helicopter. It was olivey greeney colour and it had the Yugoslav flag on it -- all these things that mark of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These men wearing red berets, what types of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore this olivey green camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When they came from the helicopter where did they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably into the barracks because they landed on the barracks ground and they must have entered the barracks buildings. They had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When they landed there, were there any other military personnel waiting for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they also wore uniforms, not the camouflage uniforms but the regular JNA uniforms. They were standing there maybe some 50 metres or 70 or 100 metres away from the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you a say a regular JNA uniform, could you describe for us what colour that was, what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the camouflage uniforms are various colours. They were not worn for regular duties, and those people who were wearing these regular uniforms that are worn every day, sort of a grey, olivey grown colour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At the time you saw these men in red berets getting off the helicopter, did you know what unit they were assigned to or what type of unit they were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I saw this camouflage uniform before in the JNA, but I had never seen before these with red berets. Maybe they belonged to some special kind of unit, but while I was in the military I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you later learn what type of unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And from whom did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that gentleman that freed me from Luka, the camp of Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Captain Rade Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I say that? He was a captain of a unit, of a military police unit of the JNA for special purposes. That is what it was called. That is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He told you what about the red berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That those were members of those special units of the JNA and they are under direct command. Above him were the Captain Dragan's soldiers that came from Serbia. That is what he told me later on when I met him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After this occasion when you saw these men with red berets coming from the helicopters, did you continue to see helicopters landing at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw that. After that usually they used to come during the night, so they would wake us up because the helicopters were noisy. Then we would go out on the balcony and look on the barracks premises.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you looked at these helicopters landing, did you see anything being taken off or put on these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On many occasions I saw them take off some boxes from there or sometimes they would put something back on the helicopter. I saw that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These red berets that you spoke of, after seeing them land in the compound did you ever see them in the Brcko area after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them in the barracks premises almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were they doing when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were training some soldiers, our neighbours. They trained them to put police handcuffs on arms. Some of them must have played the role of the victims, so he would pretend to fall down and then they would put a pistol to his head. Those special units, and then have to deal if you are attacked with a knife or how to arrest, those kinds of things, and jumping over some obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The men who were being trained, what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them, those that played the role of the victim and the instructors, they were all dressed in those camouflage SMB JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that some of these were your neighbours. Did you recognise any of these men being trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from the building where I lived there were at least six people, and also some local people, some Serbs from Brcko that in that case were voluntaries -- volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: All of these men that you recognised, the men that you knew, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 30th April, do you recall two bridges being blown up in Brcko on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before those bridges were blown up, did the town of Brcko receive any ultimatums or orders from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the only ultimatum was that the municipality should split up in a Serb municipality of Brcko, the Croatian municipality of Brcko and the Muslim municipality of Brcko. That was an ultimatum given by the members of the SDS party in the parliament of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When they made this demand for a separation, did they indicate what the boundaries would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They drew the boundaries and all the people in the town knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What areas of the town, if you remember, would come under Serb control based on their demand for a separation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly those were the Serb villages that were on the eastern side of the town of Brcko, partly on the south-eastern part of the town of Brcko, and that boundary, that separation line in the town, ended somewhere in the very centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The areas of the town that the Serbs wanted included in their section, to your knowledge, were these areas of the town that were predominantly Serb in their population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The others or the other nationalities and minorities lived there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the SDS leaders explain what these other minorities should do or the other nationalities should do once the separation was effected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not explain anything that would happen to the others.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that they gave an ultimatum that this was to be accomplished by a certain date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they indicate anything about what might happen if their demand was not met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not say anything concretely. They said that this separation had to be done by 4th May 1992, and after that no negotiations would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the response of the other groups to this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer was such that the others negotiated at the meetings of the parliament of the municipality. They negotiated with them but, as far as I know, for the most part, the people who were in the municipality parliament were for not that -- not to split the town or the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 30th April were those negotiations ongoing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not going on. I know that that was interrupted publicly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How was it represented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were following those meetings of the municipality parliament through the local Brcko TV station. We could all see that all the delegates separated and they split up and they never met again, I think.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The two bridges that were blown up on 30th April, did you ever learn who was involved in blowing up those bridges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: From whom did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Mr. Rade Bozic that freed me from Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This was the JNA captain that you spoke of earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was that captain, JNA captain.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he tell about the blowing up of these bridges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, he said that he was responsible for that and that he was commanding that operation of the blowing up of both bridges over the Sava River, and that he was really sorry because he had made a great mistake.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably what he thought was if he thought of the civilians that were killed, that were blown up together with the bridge, that old bridge over the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This bridge that his unit blew up, it connected Brcko with what town, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of those bridges on the River of Sava join us and connect us to the Republic of Croatia. There are no towns that are near. The nearest town in Croatia is Zupanja and right across us there is just a small village called Gunja.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was this pedestrian bridge used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly for pedestrians, mostly for pedestrians and for some lighter motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 30th April after the bridge was blown up, did you take your family from the town on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I took them away.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you receive any assistance in doing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of my neighbours helped me. His flat is right underneath mine.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb. He is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he or his wife say anything about the attack on Brcko that day, on the bridges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said my wife refused to leave the town. This lady neighbour of mine arrived to our flat very early in the morning and she said: "Jasminka, you have to leave the town".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did she say why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, she said.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Because the war has broken out, Jasminka", she said.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you take your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Bijeljina, in a different town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you yourself come back then to Brcko that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I came back because they called us to go and work, all the men, because there was a work duty.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who called you to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they blew the bridges up on the Sava River, I went to my company because it was a working day. So, the manager of the company told us that we should be at our homes because work duty had been introduced.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 30th April and the following days did you see soldiers in the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What types of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All kinds of uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army, from camouflage uniforms to reserve uniforms to normal regular uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the next few days did the attack on Brcko continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war broke out in Brcko on 3rd May. This was a real clash and it went on all the time while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was happening to the town? How was it being attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town, in the very centre of the town, nothing was going on, only in the access routes to town, in those parts like the Dizdarusa, Vikici or Meraje, there you could hear infantry ruffles very concretely. That was on 3rd May.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this time, 30th April until 3rd May, did you see any type of fighter aircraft in the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were two aeroplanes that had flown, I think, from the south east, somewhere from that direction between the 4th or 6th May. They flew in and then they flew towards the north western part of the town. They were flying very low, and soon afterwards one could hear a very strong detonation and the whole town was shaken. I do not know what they were aiming to shoot at, but that was somewhere in the north western part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In this area towards which they were flying, if you know, what was the ethnic group of the people that lived in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know mostly those people were Muslims and Croats, the absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that these aircraft were flying very low, were you able to distinguish colour or markings on the planes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The marking was "U", "JU", and there was the old Yugoslav flag on the hind part of that, of that aircraft, so that it means that those aircraft belonged to the JNA at that time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After 30th April, were the inhabitants of Brcko given any sort of orders or messages by the Serb leaders who had taken over the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only message was on 1st May in the morning and I saw it on the local television and it came from the President of the municipality, Mr. Captain Petrovic. He introduced himself as the captain of the army unit, of the military police Force security, and they transmitted the message that his unit had been given the mandate to take over the control of Brcko within 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After 30th April, were the people in Brcko free to move about as they wished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they could move about. In those parts of the town where I was, well, I moved around.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you able to remain in your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in my home until May 10th.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that date what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day people from my company came and took me because we were under labour directions in my company.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were taken where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to Elektrodistribucija, Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After 10th May did you remain at your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Till 27th May, 27th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened to you on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning of 27th May, police came wearing the uniforms of the civilian police and they took me to the police Station in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about the time period from 30th April until 27th May when you were arrested. During that time period were you free to move about in the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. I moved about.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After 10th May when you were taken to your work, what duties did you have to perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went removing failures on transmission lines in the town which were damaged, I guess, due to the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So during this time, between 30th April and 27th May, when you were free to move about the town of Brcko, during that time, did you see any persons killed in the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the immediate vicinity when they shot civilians in the street.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 7th May at 11 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one part of town called Stari Grad I saw civilians being shot in the middle of the street in groups of four to six to seven persons fired at, shot by men wearing camouflage uniforms of a grey olive green colour, and in the same place on the same spot they killed three men. They were killed by members of the civilian police in uniforms, that is, one of them shot three of them. He fired behind their backs, at the back of their heads.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These other groups of civilians who were killed, how were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In these two groups, they lined them up against a wall, and surrounded them in a semicircle and fired from automatic rifles at stomach or chest level. I could not really tell you where they hit them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the same time period did you see any dead bodies, other than these groups that you saw killed, in the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 12th May in front of the gymnasium "Partizan" near Hotel Galeb in a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were far away from us. We were in a car, in a company car.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see what kind of clothing they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the killed ones?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilians, they were civilians, they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where this group of bodies was located, did you see any persons in military or police uniforms in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in front of the Galeb Hotel in camouflage SMB uniforms, in front of the Galeb Hotel, not where they, those people were lying dead, but very near.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there any other occasion where you saw dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near to where my company was, they dug out a hole with a bulldozer with an excavator, as a matter of fact, and on an occasion we were working there and they were -- they brought them in a truck and unloaded them there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you see what kind of truck they brought them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sure I did, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of truck was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a truck used for meat, for the meat industry in Brcko, painted white, a white truck with a freezer. It was used for meat, to transport meat.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see who was unloading these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three of them in camouflage grey, olive green uniforms, but I did not know, I could not recognise any of them. They were too far away.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see what was done after these bodies were unloaded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the bulldozers covered that hole that was dug out, that is, covered it with the earth that was next to the hole.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that were you arrested on 27th May by two police officers, I believe. Did you recognise these police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them before the war very well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stevo Knezevic and Dragan Pantelic, and the latter was a professional policeman before the war in Brcko SUP and the other one was a member of a sports club in Brcko, or shooting club.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was their ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you said you were taken to the SUP by these two police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I ended up in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the gate, at the entrance, to my company were those two, put plastic handcuffs on me but fixed them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did they transport you to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The car, a Renault, before the war it was used by Interplet, which is a textile industry. It was used to carry textiles, to transport textiles. So they put me in the back and took me to the SUP in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long did they hold you at the SUP in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not more than an hour in that room without any light, closed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did they take you from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the SUP they took me to Luka. It is a site on the bank of the Sava, huge hangar. They took me there again in a civilian car belonging to an enterprise or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This time they wore the uniforms of the reserve JNA, two of them. I know one of them, it was a local neighbour, a Serb from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held at this Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Luka camp, I was from 27th May until 7th July 1992. I left at 4 or 5 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us a bit about the conditions in this camp? What type of food did you receive and how often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On concrete, sometimes there was perhaps some cardboard, some cardboard packaging, to cover but normally we used to -- we lied on concrete. The food, well, there were no, you know what I mean, plates or spoons. We had to use our hands to eat from some boxes, from tins.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many meals a day did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One or two while I was there or, perhaps, sometimes none while I was there per day.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at the camp was the camp guarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were guards.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did these guards wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards were outside the hangers, around those hangars, and they again wore reserve JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there other camp personnel who were located inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did these individuals wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some wore police uniforms, and there were also some in camouflage uniforms who came from time to time to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of these camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do. The one who received us the first day and then continued to call our names out every night or in the morning by name and surname, I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used to call him call Kole but his name is Konstantin Simonovic, Kosta.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is his ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb. He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his position at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time he was fond of saying that he was the Commander of the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time you were at Luka were there other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were a number.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of these other detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of them. I knew many of them there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of these men that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Muslims, most of them, and a few Croats, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at the Luka what was the gender of the people being held at that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly, when I say "mostly", men but there was a woman. There was one woman I remember well. She was released. But mostly they were men.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time you were at Luka camp, did you see anyone physically abused or killed at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Physically mistreated, I watched that often, and on an occasion I watched when they killed two at least, what I saw, and there were four in the group.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see the people who were physically abusing the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was doing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on an occasion some four or five of them broke in, those in the camouflage uniforms, and then they started beating all around with whatever they could lay their hands on, sticks, metal objects, just hitting out at random. They were strangers, they were not local Serbs from Brcko; and, as for killings, one of them was my neighbour from the building where I live.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: By that do you mean one of the victims was your neighbour or one of the perpetrators was your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the perpetrators, one of the Serb soldiers, the one who killed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb. He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time you were at Luka camp, do you recall seeing a detainee named Ibrahim Levic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he slept next to me; next to me he slept.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know him from before you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew what he looked like, but I did not know his name. I met him, that is, I learned his name and surname in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident involving him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one came in a camouflage uniform, took a knife, grabbed him by the neck and incised a cross in his forehead with a knife.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This person who came and did that, had you ever seen this person in the camp before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came all the time. He was one of the more prominent who was very fond of hitting or striking or beating the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What type of military uniform did he wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage, SMB uniform.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he have any type of insignia or patches on that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so, but he was fond of introducing himself as, and that is what he called himself, a member of the radical party from Bijeljina, a Chetnik. That is how he used to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Had you heard of this party before that called itself "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had heard of the Serb radical party before the war, but at that time they did not call themselves Chetniks. It started down there in the camp when they began to use that terminology.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the leader of that party was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know in Yugoslavia and I know at local levels also.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was the higher level leader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Vojislav Seselj in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And your local leader?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of those whom I met in Brcko there was Mirko Blagojevic. They called him "Vojvoda". He was the President of the Radical Party in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to this one man who said he was a Chetnik, were there other paramilitary members who came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came, many of them wearing different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you learn what paramilitary units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that with certainty because they introduced themselves and their insignia, of course, were quite telling.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What paramilitary units did they introduce themselves as belonging to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Serb Volunteer Guard, Arkan's Tigers. I repeat, that is what they called themselves, Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about Major Mauser and his group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did many times and I met him and I met him once.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you meet him in Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not come to Luka while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you meet Major Mauser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the premises in the yard of my company where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know it was Major Mauser?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman introduced himself, lined us up ---

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and, as he put it, delivered a lecture to us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was this lecture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About how he had lost a couple of his wounded soldiers who died on operating tables in the town hospital, because there was not enough power, electrical energy, in that part of the town. He thought that we were responsible for it, but we could not gain access to that part of the town. Then he put a pistol on the neck and threatened us: "If it happens again, I'll kill you, all Turks, balija", and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You have mentioned that in the camp people were abused by individuals wearing military uniforms and by individuals who identified themselves with paramilitary groups. In addition to that, did you ever see any of the guards or camp personnel abuse people in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The guards, our guards, were outside the building, they never abused anyone. But those in multi-coloured uniforms, they were the ones who mistreated us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at Luka camp, did you ever see any dead bodies in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have to take part in disposing of some of these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, three or four of them came into the hangar and Kosta was with them and they were looking for volunteers. Now, some people stepped out of their own will to go and do something.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you selected to be a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one said: "Well, you look well, I think you can work well, come along".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we went out and the other side of the hangar we passed through another hangar and came out towards the bank of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you find there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a group of dead bodies in a pile, and those who brought us there, those soldiers, they said: "Well, now grab them by the arms and the legs and throw them into the water".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I threw two of them into the water.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were these bodies wearing, what type of clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, dressed normally, as I am now, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the gender of these deceased persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Men, they were all men.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see any injuries or wounds on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was holes in their backs and on the head here, and puddles of blood.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you certain that all of these people were dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them opened his eyes when we turned him around and took him to throw him away to the water, he opened the eyes. It seems to me that he was alive, but I may be wrong. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you tell the military persons with you that one of them appeared to be alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no time because they started the fire from Croatia, whether against us or the Serb soldiers, so they hid behind those wagons and I lied down. I wanted to run towards the hangars, and one of the guards said: "Why do we not shoot these too? Fuck their mother", and another one said: "Well, let them go, let them run, let them save their life".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When they said, "Why do we not shoot these two", were they referring to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were not two of us, there were several of us there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So they were referring to the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These people who took you to remove these bodies, were these regular camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, those who were on the outside, I did not know where they came, but they were wearing camouflage uniforms, but they used to come even before that incident.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, in that group there were all others. I do not know if they were from the town, whether they were Serbs from Brcko; one of them was, but he did not come with us to that place where we were disposing of the bodies. He had stayed behind probably with Kosta in the office, and there was a Serb from Brcko with them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you yourself mistreated at Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before you continue into that line of questioning, we will stand in recess, please, for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are waiting for Defence counsel. We have completed our recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I apologise for being so late, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Are you ready to proceed, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Gasi, before the recess, I had asked you if while you were at Luka camp you yourself were mistreated and you had begun to answer that. Could you tell us, please, were you mistreated while you were at that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian]: Yes, I was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was done to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first day upon my arrival when they took me there, one of those, his name was Ivan, he entered into the middle of the hangar. There were two others with him dressed in the same way wearing grey olive camouflage uniforms. They were standing behind him and they were carrying automatic weapons, and he also held a metal object in his hands. Then he entered into the middle of the hangar and he asked: "Where is that Shiptar Albanian who arrived today?"

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: By that did he mean you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first moment I did not realise whether he meant myself because I saw another prisoner on the other side, his father was also Albanian, so I was not too sure who he meant.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after he asked that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He repeated the question once again, and then I stood up and then he said: "Come here, near me."

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came near him, he waved with his hand that contained a metal object, I think it must have been a wrench for the fire hose, and he waved it, I think, to hit me in my head, but I stepped aside and then he missed, and then he waved again with that wrench, and then I stepped aside once again and he hit me in my other shoulder and then I fell down not completely but on my knees. One of those two men behind him said: "You can't knock him down by just one blow," meaning that I was so strong that he could not knock me down just by giving me one blow, and then he started to kick me with his feet. At some stage he kicked me with his feet, with his military boot, into my head and for a moment I think I fell unconscious, and then ---

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- one of those men accompanying him, he came behind my back and made me stand up and then Ivan took a pistol out, triggered it and put it into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he pulled the trigger, but did not shoot. Then he said that I was lucky because on this occasion he did not have a bullet for me, but he would have it on another occasion, and then he, the other man let me go and I fell down on my knees and hands and then he said: "I will come again, you are free for now."

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said the man that did this to you was named Ivan; was he a regular camp guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was -- he belonged to that group of men who used to come to the camp. He was not one of the guards that guarded the camp from the outside. He used to come from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever learn what group he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, I do not think I know because I asked later on. One of those people accompanying him were wearing insignia of the Serbian Volunteers Guard. They were called like that at that time, Arkan's soldiers. He was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is that insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What they call real Arkan's men, they wore on the left-hand side of their uniform the flag of the Republic of Serbia, and on their sleeves they also wore the same small insignia and they also wore heads of tigers, a drawing of a tiger's head, and it was written the "Serb guard" on one of those uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were at Luka camp did any military officers come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at one occasion they came driven in a blue Golf belonging to the police, the police that existed before the war. That Golf pulled up in front of the door of the camp, Luka, and it was written ,"The Republic Secretariat for the Interior of the Republic of Serbia" with the old coat of arms of the Republic of Serbia, and that gentleman was wearing a camouflage grey olive uniform. He did not have any cap on his head. He was accompanied by two civilian policemen that also wore the insignia of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, and the other one had the Federal Ministry of the Interior insignia, and they came into the hangar, and then Kosta came into the hangar because he was probably surprised to see them there and they entered the hangar and they went into the middle of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then what happened after they came into the middle of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He then asked, Kosta arrived in the meantime, he asked: "Kosta, let me see those", as he said, "the Muslim sniper man; I heard you had two of them here".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then Kosta said : "They are there in the corner of the hangar down there". Those two men were lying on some kind of a sport type of mattress. They were sleeping on that mattress, two men I know from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened with these two men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Major who accompanied Kosta and the other two stood in front of them and he asked the first gentleman, "Why are you here in Luka, in this camp, why are you detained here?"

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did the man say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said more or less, "To tell me, to say to me that I am some kind of a Muslim sniper man; I am not that, Major".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were these two men abused by the people who came or by Kosta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure for Kosta, but Goran Jelisic regularly beat, and when I say "regularly", that means non-stop during the day, some five times per day and regularly before going to bed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Major and the two policemen who came in this blue vehicle, did they do anything with these two men who had been identified as snipers? Did they take them from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not do anything to them, but the Major only said: "Kosta, fuck you. If the Muslim snipers are like that, I would not lose a single of my soldiers in Brcko. You have to bring, call a doctor straight away to give some medical care to those people", and really the next day came a doctor that simply with some clean water washed them. We could not have any other kind of care in Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion when you were with Kosta and there was a 2nd Lieutenant with Kosta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was with Kosta, that was not a 2nd Lieutenant, but he wore the insignia. His name was Goran Jelisic. I was taken to Kosta's office during the night and he had the insignia of a 2nd Lieutenant.
